newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Frayed Albanian army begins battle to reorganise.
newsitem.headline: Frayed Albanian army begins battle to reorganise.

text.p: Albania's army, which virtually disintegrated earlier this year, began the battle to reorganise itself on Monday in what officers said was a sign of hope and peace.

"This is the first unit that has been reorganised in the whole army," said Major General Ali Koceku of the First Infantry Battalion of Durres after a ceremony in this port city, where a multinational security force was expected to land on Tuesday.
"The message that this unit brings is very important for all of Albania and all of the army," he told reporters after the event, attended by Defence Minister Shaqir Vukaj.
"It's a message of peace. It's a message for the future, for the reorganisation of the Albanian army. It's a message of support for the new Albanian government."
Inexperienced troops in old-fashioned khaki uniforms carrying Kalashnikov rifles struggled to stay in line as they paraded past their compound to the sound of an army band.
Their belts had big brass buckles embossed with a star, a symbol of the former Stalinist regime which collapsed in 1990.
Discipline was lax. One soldier slouched and yawned and another had his helmet slung over his bayonet.
"They're not very well organised," admitted Koceku.
But he added: "The most important thing about today is to give them back the necessary motivation."

Vukaj said the reason for his trip to Durres, where the main contingent of the eight-nation Italian-led force to protect aid convoys was due to arrive from Tuesday, was show solidarity with his troops.
"The principal aim was to boost the morale of the soldiers," he told reporters. "We are working to reorganise the army in all of Albania and we hope we will succeed."
Soldiers in Durres deserted for up to two weeks last month when the unrest that swept Albania after the collapse of a number of fraudulent savings schemes was at its peak.
"On the worst day, everyone else left so I did too," said one of the soldiers, who declined to give his name.

Vukaj looked on as the troops from the 400-strong battalion, some joking and chatting, stood to attention near ancient-looking tanks. Others, stripped to the waist in the sunshine, were doing pull-ups on bars in an exercise field.
The sprawling compound escaped relatively unscathed in February when a number of army in other parts of the country were looted.
People grabbed rifles and ammunition and rebel committees were set up as the south slid out of government control.

President Sali Berisha, who has agreed to call early elections by the end of June, installed a new government of national unity headed by opposition Socialist leader Bashkim Fino a month ago. It has succeeded in restoring some calm.
In contrast to Albania's ragged army, the U.N.-backed security force includes 6,000 troops from Italy, France, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Romania, Austria and Denmark.
Koceku said the mission to distribute emergency food aid and medicines was vital. "But more important is the effect of stabilisation and security that it will produce," he said.
"I think their humanitarian mission is secondary compared to that."
